## Curriculum draft
This syllabus sketches a spring project seminar around LeRobot, the SO-101, and the Arduino UNO Q. The weekly table is a proposed arm-centered sequence, subject to a tested STM32-to-servo command path, a local policy pilot, and a reproduced arm station. The [one-axis reference sequence](../../labs/vol4/lab-sequence.md) is the fallback if the arm path cannot be qualified. These are design briefs, not released assignments. The teaching team must measure the chosen rig before setting kit requirements, timing thresholds, or enrollment capacity. The [Volume IV manuscript](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol4/) is also in active development.
:::

## Course at a glance

| | |
|:---|:---|
| **Format** | Two meetings per teaching week: a short systems framing and student-led trace discussion, then an Andrea-led project lab. One semester project per team; weekly studio prompts and four graded milestones. No written exam. |
| **Duration** | 14 teaching weeks across ETH's spring term, with the class-free Easter week left open |
| **Prior draft identifiers** | Harvard CS/EE 288 · ETH Zurich 151-0851; confirm before course adoption |
| **Prior draft credits** | 4 Harvard credits / 6 ECTS; confirm against local workload rules |
| **Audience** | Advanced undergraduate or graduate students with programming, operating systems, basic probability, and introductory machine learning or control experience |
| **Team** | Two or three students per station, subject to the hardware pilot |
| **Text** | *Physical AI: Machine Learning Systems That Sense and Act* (Volume IV) |
| **Hardware** | Arduino UNO Q, staff-qualified SO-101 arm and camera, STM32-mediated motor command path, independent motor-power cutoff, and a low-energy task fixture; final parts list pending pilot. A guarded one-axis station is the fallback governed rig. |
| **Workload** | Provisional 90-minute seminar and three-hour lab each teaching week, plus team build, analysis, and focused reading. Weekly notebook updates replace separate lab reports; set the final timetable and credit allocation with the ETH course listing. |

## How the semester project runs

The first six meetings establish a common system path: calibrate the body, record episodes, compare a baseline, run a learned model on the UNO Q, and close a measured feedback loop. The week-6 minimum demonstration is a guarded learned reach followed by a safe scene change or incomplete move; the new observation must alter the next proposal or justify abstention. A complete grasp is not required for this demonstration. Teams choose a task by week 2 and apply each common experiment to that same task. Weeks 7–14 are project studios: teams compare simulation with hardware, pursue a chosen policy investigation, measure timing, handle faults, rehearse, and defend a final physical trial. The linked labs are prompts for the same project; weeks 8–9 offer a choice, week 12 allows repair, and week 13 is a rehearsal buffer. The [course operating plan](../../labs/vol4/course-architecture.md) specifies the project milestones and evidence; the [fourteen lab blueprints](../../labs/vol4/lab-blueprints.md) specify possible experiments; the [competency matrix](../../labs/vol4/student-competencies.md) states what each student must demonstrate independent of hardware choice.

Each week starts with a prediction from the reading and ends with a brief shared notebook entry: a raw trace or replayable episode, measured outcome, discrepancy, and next experiment, with code and model revisions linked when relevant. Staff check this evidence at the bench without a separate weekly grade. The four graded milestones are a week-2 task charter, a week-6 running feedback loop, a week-10 action-permission test, and a week-14 unfamiliar physical trial and report. The team submits one system, while each student explains their own measurements and a selected fault trace at the final defense.

The seminar meeting begins with a short systems framing and a rotating student-led critique of one claim from the reading and one team's actual trace. Peers ask what the trace proves and which alternative explanation remains. The studio then applies that question to each team's project. The seminar rewards a defensible negative result and a clear revision of the project claim.

## Two meetings each week

**Meeting A, systems seminar (about 90 minutes):** Professor Reddi frames one physical AI question in 10–15 minutes. A rotating team then discusses a focused section of the linked chapter and presents one raw trace or failed prediction from its project. Peers challenge the measurement, physical assumptions, and authority path. Close by stating the experiment each team will run in lab. A research paper is background unless it directly serves a project question; no separate paper presentation is required.

**Meeting B, supervised project lab (about three hours):** Dr. Garavagno leads the station briefing on safe state, motion limits, and one common measurement. Teams then spend most of the block collecting data, changing their system, or running trials on their own project. Short bench reviews end with a trace, a result or documented failure, and a next experiment. Teams update their shared notebook afterward; only the four milestones require graded packets. The staff pilot sets enrollment and reservation capacity.

The capstone begins with the week-2 project charter. Students may choose the physical question, baseline, model, simulator, and recovery strategy within a staff-qualified station and operating envelope. The common requirements remain a local learned action proposal, MCU permission, consequential physical feedback, a changed-state decision, matched baseline, and fault evidence. A new embodiment or sensor module is welcome only after staff qualify it. Weeks 7–12 give teams increasing discretion over methods; the linked labs supply questions and minimum evidence, not identical solutions.

## Required reading and lab materials

The weekly table links to the relevant Volume IV chapters. Staff identify one core section for discussion; when two chapters appear, the second is background unless announced otherwise. Each row also links to a studio brief, which gives the experiment and evidence standard even when that week's work is formative or optional. LeRobot technical documentation is an implementation reference supplied where needed in the qualified station instructions. No external robotics course or tutorial is assigned as reading for this offering.

## The semester project

Teams choose a **small physical AI loop** in the opening weeks and develop it on a staff-qualified SO-101 station. The common reference project is a disturbance-and-recovery manipulation cell: the arm moves toward a soft block or marked destination, staff safely alter the scene or cause an incomplete move, and the system must use the resulting observation to revise its action or abstain. A successful grasp and placement is an extension after the guarded reach works. Each project must pass the book's [Physical AI scope test](../../books/vol4/01_boundary/01_boundary.qmd): a learned model, consequential physical feedback, and delegated actuator authority. A versioned Hugging Face model runs locally on the UNO Q's Qualcomm processor and influences the bounded action proposal. The STM32 microcontroller permits or refuses it; the system measures the actual tool and object state before deciding again. Teams compare this loop with a scripted baseline on matched physical disturbances. Model inference alone, or a camera label followed by a fixed arm script, does not pass.

Candidate SO-101 projects include **instruction-conditioned sorting**, **active inspection before grasping**, and **recovery from an incomplete grasp or placement**. These are prompts rather than assigned tasks. Teams submit a physical goal, preliminary envelope, measurement plan, baseline, and fallback by week 2; week 6 is the first running-system demonstration. Training, simulation, and analysis may use a workstation. The course uses LeRobot's episode and policy workflow throughout. Additional mobile or thermal projects require separately qualified stations. Staff will pilot local SmolVLA inference on the UNO Q before deciding whether a VLA rollout can be required of every team.

The UNO Q combines a Qualcomm QRB2210 Linux processor with an STM32U585 microcontroller and provides Bridge communication between them ([Arduino UNO Q documentation](https://docs.arduino.cc/hardware/uno-q/), [datasheet](https://docs.arduino.cc/resources/datasheets/ABX00162-datasheet.pdf)). [Hugging Face LeRobot](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/lerobot-dataset-v3) provides the course's episode and policy workflow: demonstrations become versioned data, then a policy is evaluated in simulation and on the physical station. The first on-board model may be a compact visual or action policy exported with [Optimum ONNX](https://huggingface.co/docs/optimum-onnx/onnx/usage_guides/export_a_model) and run on the QRB2210 CPU. Staff must prove that path and separately measure [SmolVLA](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/smolvla) on the exact board. Qualcomm AI Hub performance reported for other devices is not a UNO Q measurement. [ACT](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/act) supplies a smaller imitation-policy exercise. The stock [SO-101 USB motor-bus connection](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/so101) does not give the UNO Q's STM32 per-command authority, so an arm capstone must qualify that path separately.

ETH's [academic calendar](https://ethz.ch/staffnet/en/news-and-events/academic-calendar.html) places spring teaching in calendar weeks 8–22, including one class-free week after Easter. This sequence uses 14 teaching meetings; dates and submission rules should follow the actual course listing.

## Learning outcomes

By the end of the course, students should be able to:

1. Draw a complete sensing-to-actuation path and identify which components may propose, permit, and execute a physical action.
2. Calibrate independent sensors, measure actuator travel, power-off state, duty limits, and end-to-end latency, then set an operating envelope from those measurements.
3. Use a shared observation/action contract in multiple simulations; compare predicted trajectories with held-out physical traces and evaluate a learned next-state model.
4. Record and audit robot episodes, train and version a policy, deploy a learned model locally, compare it with a nonlearned baseline, and analyze reactive and sequence actions.
5. Distinguish offline model metrics from physical task outcomes, including correction error, abstention, incomplete motion, and failed recovery.
6. Implement and test action permission, intervention, and recovery under stale requests, component faults, and compute load; defend a bounded release or no-release claim with trace evidence.

## Weekly studio sequence

Every week produces evidence used by the next. The seminar turns a focused reading into a prediction; the lab measures the real rig or a recorded trace and explains the gap. Staff supply a qualified SO-101 reference station and starter artifacts so students can reach a physical feedback loop by week 6. Teams choose a project by week 2. The linked lab briefs are prompts and evidence standards, not separate graded submissions; they remain drafts until the staff pilot supplies exact commands and motion limits. The [student competency checklist](../../labs/vol4/student-competencies.md) defines platform-independent outcomes.

| Week | Reading source | Studio prompt |
|---:|---|---|
| 1–2 | [Ch. 1: The Causal Boundary](../../books/vol4/01_boundary/01_boundary.qmd); [Ch. 2: The Physical Body](../../books/vol4/02_body/02_body.qmd) | [Lab 1: The Causal Boundary & Servo Bus Bring-Up](../../labs/vol4/lab-01-boundary.md) |
| 3 | [Ch. 3: The Cognitive Brain](../../books/vol4/03_brain/03_brain.qmd); [Ch. 4: The Nervous System](../../books/vol4/04_nervous/04_nervous.qmd) | [Lab 2: Multi-Modal Sensing & The Inter-Core Bridge](../../labs/vol4/lab-02-body-and-sensors.md) |
| 4–5 | [Ch. 5: Physical Data](../../books/vol4/05_data/05_data.qmd); [Ch. 7: Closed-Loop Evaluation](../../books/vol4/07_evaluation/07_evaluation.qmd) | [Lab 3: Teleoperation, LeRobot Dataset & Action Taps](../../labs/vol4/lab-03-physical-episodes.md) |
| 6 | [Ch. 6: Policy Training](../../books/vol4/06_training/06_training.qmd) | [Lab 4: Deterministic Baseline & SmolVLA/ACT Export](../../labs/vol4/lab-04-baseline-and-learning.md) |
| 7–8 | [Ch. 8: Sensor Perception](../../books/vol4/08_perception/08_perception.qmd); [Ch. 11: Trajectory Planning](../../books/vol4/11_planning/11_planning.qmd); [Ch. 13: Silicon Placement](../../books/vol4/13_placement/13_placement.qmd) | [Lab 5: Autonomous Closed-Loop Reach on UNO Q](../../labs/vol4/lab-05-local-feedback-loop.md) |
| 9 | [Ch. 10: Grounded Intent](../../books/vol4/10_intent/10_intent.qmd); [Ch. 12: Safety Enforcement](../../books/vol4/12_enforcement/12_enforcement.qmd) | [Lab 6: Action Horizons, Language & Disturbances](../../labs/vol4/lab-06-action-chunks.md) |
| 10 | [Ch. 12: Safety Enforcement](../../books/vol4/12_enforcement/12_enforcement.qmd); [Ch. 14: Supervisory Intervention](../../books/vol4/14_intervention/14_intervention.qmd) | [Lab 7: The Microcontroller Safety Governor](../../labs/vol4/lab-07-authority-under-fault.md) |
| 11 | [Ch. 15: Adversarial Verification](../../books/vol4/15_verification/15_verification.qmd); [Ch. 16: Deployment Release](../../books/vol4/16_release/16_release.qmd) | [Lab 8: Fault Injection & Fail-Safe Cutoffs](../../labs/vol4/lab-08-verification-and-release.md) |
| 12–14 | [Ch. 1–17: Volume IV Core Curriculum](../../books/vol4/17_frontier/17_frontier.qmd) | [Capstone Project Studio & Release Defense](../../labs/vol4/lab-capstone-studio.md) |

Week 9 explores action horizons and language conditioning, while week 11 verifies fail-safe cutoffs before the 3-week Capstone studio. The chapters are **reading sources**, not a requirement to implement every mechanism they discuss. Larger VLAs, diffusion policies, 3D scene memory, field-oriented control, EtherCAT, seqlocks, and kilohertz CBF-QP may be examined in seminar or simulation. SmolVLA is an explicit staff deployment experiment on the UNO Q; a student VLA rollout depends on its measured memory and timing and on a qualified actuator command path. The SO-101 exercises the book's manipulation class; mobility and process/energy principles require separately qualified bodies or simulation comparisons. The studio makes claims only about mechanisms students implement and measure on their rigs.

## Assessment

| Component | Weight | Evidence |
|:---|---:|:---|
| Task charter and safe station signoff (week 2) | 15% | Bounded physical task, baseline, outcome measure, operating envelope, and authority diagram |
| Local feedback loop (week 6) | 25% | Learned proposal on the Q, MCU permission, measured scene change, revised decision or abstention, and matched rule trial |
| Authority under fault (week 10) | 20% | MCU refusal of stale and invalid proposals, operator cutoff, and measured no-motion result |
| Capstone system report and defense (week 14) | 40% | Concise report, repeated physical trials, baseline comparison, fault result, tested envelope, and individual trace explanation |

Weekly notebook updates, seminar participation, and the week-13 rehearsal receive formative feedback. The report draws on those records; students do not submit fourteen separate lab reports.

A good model metric cannot compensate for a bypassed interlock or unexplained physical motion. The teaching team may require a repair and repeat trial before a project advances. The final verdict describes a **course prototype within a tested envelope**, not a certified safety system.

## Preparation before offering the course

The teaching team should first test the complete Hugging Face model path on the exact UNO Q variant: pinned model and preprocessing, host-versus-board output check, camera capture, local inference on the QRB2210, Bridge proposal, MCU permission, bounded SO-101 motion, and a second observation. Build and reproduce the one-joint and whole-arm STM32-to-servo command path with no live host bypass; test camera and joint feedback, power-off behavior, and end-to-end latency under load. Prepare LeRobot episodes, two pinned simulation fixtures and the ACT exercise, and a separate local SmolVLA feasibility report. Start from the [candidate kit and cost sheet](../../labs/vol4/kit-bom.md), then record the tested bill of materials, wiring, software versions, assembly instructions, spares, station booking plan, and replay path for outages. The [feasibility plan](../../labs/vol4/feasibility-plan.md) gives the work and evidence for every week; the [SO-101 course draft](../../labs/vol4/so101-uno-q-course.md) gives the hardware tests. If the arm command path does not work, use the one-axis reference station for the STM32-controlled loop and keep the arm for LeRobot data and policy exercises. Publish numeric timing and motion thresholds only after the pilot.
